name: VL6180X time-of-flight rangefinder breakout
//: A carrier for ST's VL6180X. WHICH carrier matters more than usual and most of the unknowns below are about that, not about the chip.

needs.note: Only needed if the sensor is to wake the host from sleep. It ranges continuously by itself and asserts this pin on a threshold, which is the only way a sleeping host can be told about a hand.

power.note: the carrier regulates down to the die's 2.8 V

die_supply_v.why_it_matters: The DIE is a 2.8 V part. A bus pulled to 3.3 V meets a pad powered from 2.8 V, and whether that is safe depends entirely on whether the carrier level-shifts.

carrier_has_level_shifters.source: unknown until the exact carrier is identified
carrier_has_level_shifters.why_it_matters: Decides whether host-side pull-ups help the sensor side at all, and whether 3.3 V on the bus is safe. Adafruit 3316 and Pololu 2489 shift; cheap GY-VL6180 boards may not.

carrier_pulls_up_the_interrupt.why_it_matters: If GPIO1 is open-drain and the carrier has no pull-up, the host's interrupt pin FLOATS while awake — and a floating pin reads low about as often as not, so the lid opens at random with nothing in front of it. One meter reading settles it.

idle_current_ma.why_it_matters: It free-runs while the host sleeps, so on a battery design it is one of the two or three loads that decide the answer.

host_requirements: I2C needs pull-ups. The host's own internal pull-ups are tens of kiloohms and far too weak; size them against the bus speed and the cable, not by habit.
If this sits on a ribbon away from the board, the ribbon's capacitance is part of the bus and belongs in the rise-time budget.

Behind a window, range-ignore must be calibrated or the window's own reflection reads as a target — and on an interrupt-driven design that is a wake loop, which is worse for the battery than never sleeping.
//on_board: It has to look out through the enclosure, so it is never on the PCB. The board carries the mating header and no body is drawn for it.
